chapter_theme: Sweet speech is defined as loving, guileless and true, then ranked above generous giving. Its closing argument is almost one of common sense: why would anyone choose the unripe fruit?
structure_note: Parimelazhagar divides the chapter: what sweet speech is (91), its value especially in hospitality (92-93), its fruit in this life (94-95), in the next (96), in both (97-98), and the fault of harsh speech (99-100).

91.reading: Sweet words are those from the mouths of people who see the true thing, moist with love and free of deceit.
91.nuance: The definition rules out flattery. Sweetness needs truthfulness and love, and ஈரம், moisture, makes love a physical quality of the words. Whether it allows rebuke is what the commentators bring out.

positions.position: செம்பொருள் is virtue, and the speakers are those who understand it.
The speakers judge disputes between two parties, and they must rebuke sweetly too.
positions.quote: இஃது ஒருவனைக் கடிந்து சொல்லவேண்டு மிடத்தும் இன்சொல்லாலே கடிய வேண்டுமென்றது.

92.reading: Better than giving with a glad heart is to be, with a glad face, a person of sweet speech.
92.nuance: This is a surprising ranking in a book so committed to giving. Parimelazhagar's reasoning is that sweet speech is in one's own power, where a gift depends on wealth, yet it comes naturally only to a virtuous heart, so it's the rarer thing.

93.reading: Virtue lies in sweet words from the heart, after looking kindly with a glad face.
93.nuance: The sequence is face, then eye, then heart, then word, and அகத்தானாம் is what keeps it from being mere manners. Parimelazhagar takes the emphatic ending as 'not in giving'. That's a strong inference: the verse may only be emphasizing speech.

94.reading: Grievous want won't come to those whose sweet speech gives everyone joy.
94.nuance: The two forms உறூஉம் balance grief and joy in matching words. The promise seems to be social, not magical: Parimelazhagar reasons that one who has only friends comes to all wealth.

positions.position: துவ்வாமை is material poverty, in which the senses have nothing to enjoy.
The want removed is a poverty of friendship.

95.reading: Being humble and sweet-spoken is a person's ornament, and nothing else is.
95.nuance: The verse states humility without limit. Parimelazhagar limits it: one is to be humble toward those who deserve deference and sweet-spoken toward everybody. That's a notable narrowing by the commentator.

96.reading: If one seeks out good things and speaks them sweetly, what is not virtue wears away and virtue grows.
96.nuance: நாடி, having sought out, makes sweetness conditional on content. Parimelazhagar adds the converse: good counsel spoken harshly isn't virtue. For him the effect is on the speaker's own merit, whereas Kalaignar makes it a method of guiding others.

97.reading: Speech that yields benefit and never parts from gentleness produces justice and brings forth good.
97.nuance: பயன் and பண்பு are held together, so usefulness alone doesn't suffice and neither does charm. Parimelazhagar defines நயன் strikingly as being in accord with the world.

98.reading: Sweet speech free of pettiness gives joy in the next life and in this one.
98.nuance: The next life is named first, and Parimelazhagar says this is because its joy is greater. Kalaignar reads this as renown during and after life, which removes the afterlife. Pope's and Parimelazhagar's 'harm to others' is more specific than சிறுமை, smallness.

99.reading: Why would one who sees how sweetly sweet speech yields use harsh words?
99.nuance: Parimelazhagar makes this an argument from experience: you know how others' sweet words feel to you, and harsh words are just as painful to them. The verse doesn't command, it only asks what the point is.

100.reading: Speaking unpleasant things when pleasant ones are there is like grabbing raw fruit when ripe fruit is at hand.
100.nuance: The final charge is stupidity, not wickedness. Parimelazhagar makes the stakes much higher by reading the fruit as Avvai's nelli, which is like amrita, and the raw one as poison. He adds that harsh speech ends up hurting the speaker, and this allusion is a thread to the Sangam story of Avvai and the king.

links.note: Both use the pair அகனமர்ந்து and முகனமர்ந்து. In 84 the goddess's glad heart answers the host's glad face. In 92 the glad face outranks even the giver's glad heart, so the same pair yields a different ranking.
Sweet words here must be free of deceit. In 292, even a falsehood counts as truth if it yields blameless good. What 91 excludes by definition, 292 may allow when the outcome justifies it.

Here a pleasant word beats a gladly given gift. In 225, relieving hunger is a power above the ascetic's. A hungry person's view of 92 might differ, which suggests the ranking in 92 assumes someone who isn't in need.

Parimelazhagar limits humility in 95 to those who deserve deference. In 125, bowing is good for all and most of all for the rich, which speaks to who should bow rather than to whom, and doesn't contain his limit.
97 requires speech to be useful and gentle, and 200 says to speak only what is useful. The later chapter keeps the usefulness test and drops the sweetness, which shows the two tests are independent.

On Parimelazhagar's reading, 99 argues from how sweet words feel to oneself. 316 makes the same move in general: don't do to others what you know to be painful. The same reciprocity works for speech and for deeds.

source_issues: The Tamil of verse 98 in kg/core reads சிறுமையுவு, a typo for சிறுமையுள் as Parimelazhagar's text shows.
Manakkudavar is not aligned for verses 92, 93, 94, 95 and 98.
